tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: redb's author ran a public harness (crates/redb-bench/benches/lmdb_benchmark.rs and common.rs at commit d6773ef, the 2025-08-08 commit that last regenerated the README table) on a stated CPU (Ryzen 9950X3D), but the rustc version and the C compiler and flags for the bundled LMDB, RocksDB and SQLite are not stated, so it falls short of A. Tier B rests on the RocksDB comparison; the SQLite rows come from a handicapped adapter and include >50x ratios that on their own would cap the entry at C.

corrections.baseline: RocksDB (rust-rocksdb 0.22.0 with LZ4, 4 GiB LRU block cache, bloom filters, OptimisticTransactionDB snapshot reads); SQLite (rusqlite 0.37 bundled, default settings, BLOB PRIMARY KEY table) is also in the table, but its adapter re-prepared every SQL statement per operation (see caveats)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Times in ms, lower is better, from the redb README table (last regenerated 2025-08-08); all ratios derived from page data. Against RocksDB: random reads 637 vs 2911 (4.6x); random range reads 565 vs 2734 (4.8x); random reads with 4, 8, 16 and 32 threads 840 vs 3995 (4.8x), 427 vs 2147 (5.0x), 216 vs 1478 (6.8x) and 125 vs 1100 (8.8x); individual sync writes 1598 vs 2432 (1.5x); bulk load 9232 vs 13969 (1.5x). LMDB loses to RocksDB on batch writes (942 vs 451, 2.1x slower) and removals (10435 vs 6900, 1.5x slower), and its uncompacted file is 2.61 GiB vs 893.18 MiB (3.0x larger). Against SQLite (handicapped adapter, see caveats): random reads 637 vs 4283 (6.7x); random range reads 565 vs 8431 (14.9x); 16 and 32 threads 216 vs 23022 (107x) and 125 vs 26536 (212x); individual writes 1598 vs 7040 (4.4x); batch writes 942 vs 2625 (2.8x); bulk load 9232 vs 15341 (1.7x); removals 10435 vs 10323 (parity, LMDB 1% slower); uncompacted size 2.61 GiB vs 1.09 GiB (LMDB 2.4x larger).
corrections.workload: redb author's comparison harness as of commit d6773ef (2025-08-08): 5M random pairs (24-byte keys, 150-byte values) bulk-loaded in one transaction, 1,000 individual synchronous write transactions, 100 batches of 1,000 writes, 1M random point reads and 500k random 10-element range scans (each run twice and printed as two rows), random reads with 4, 8, 16 and 32 threads (about 5.1M lookups split across the threads), then removal of about 2.55M keys in one transaction; 4 GiB cache for the engines that take one (4 GiB map size for LMDB, no cache pragma for SQLite); LMDB driven through the Rust heed 0.22 binding.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (the bench profile inherits release optimisation; the workspace Cargo.toml adds debug = true); rustc version not stated (workspace MSRV 1.89). C compiler and flags for the bundled LMDB (heed 0.22), RocksDB (rust-rocksdb 0.22.0, lz4 feature) and SQLite (rusqlite 0.37 bundled) come from those crates' build scripts and are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a competing project's (redb) README, not from the LMDB authors, and LMDB is reached through the heed 0.22 Rust wrapper. The table was last regenerated on 2025-08-08 (commit d6773ef; the 2026-07-15 commit only removed the sled column), so it reflects that commit's harness and crate versions (rusqlite 0.37, rust-rocksdb 0.22.0), not the current crates/redb-bench-compare harness (rusqlite 0.38, rocksdb 0.24, median of 3 runs) that the README now links. At that commit the SQLite adapter called conn.prepare or execute inside every get, range scan, insert and delete, so each SQLite operation recompiled its SQL statement; SQLite also ran with no tuning pragmas (rollback journal, no WAL, default page cache of about 2 MB versus 4 GiB for redb, RocksDB and fjall), and in the threaded rows each lookup is its own autocommit statement on a per-thread connection, which likely explains why SQLite slows down as threads are added (7000 ms with 4 threads, 26536 ms with 32 threads for the same 5.1M lookups). The SQLite ratios, above all the 107x and 212x threaded ones, therefore overstate LMDB's lead over a normally used SQLite; current master prepares the read statements once per reader, but the README was not re-run. RocksDB was configured sensibly (4 GiB block cache, bloom filters, snapshot reads), and against it LMDB wins reads by 4.6-8.8x but loses batch writes and removals and uses about 3x more disk. Compiler version and flags are not stated. The primary LMDB claim, the Symas/lmdb.tech microbench against SQLite, BerkeleyDB, Kyoto Cabinet and LevelDB, could not be opened (host blocked). A second, weaker data point from Mozilla's kvbench (mykmelez/kvbench README, Rust bindings, hardware not stated) shows LMDB opening a database about 8x faster than LevelDB (166.70 us vs 1.3895 ms, derived from page data) but slower on a single synchronous 1-byte put (114.74 us vs 58.691 us).

notes: README numbers match the record, but the SQLite comparison is handicapped: the harness that produced them (commit d6773ef) re-prepared every SQL statement per call, ran SQLite untuned, and the 107x/212x threaded ratios are harness artifacts, so I rebased the baseline on RocksDB (also a category baseline, same table, sensible config: 4.6-8.8x on reads, LMDB slower on batch writes and removals) and kept SQLite rows with the flaw spelled out; tier stays B. Record shortcoming: SQLite baseline handicapped (per-call statement preparation, default cache, no WAL), README table from 2025-08 harness not current one, compiler and flags unstated. Metadata: OLDAP-2.8 (libraries/liblmdb/LICENSE), about 3.0k stars, read-only mirror of openldap.org (not a GitHub fork), last commit 2026-08-19 on default branch mdb.master3 (record said 2026-06-24), active.

tier_reason: First-party Google page (July 2011) with public benchmark code (benchmarks/db_bench.cc, db_bench_sqlite3.cc, db_bench_tree_db.cc, all still in the repo) and a stated CPU (Xeon X5650), but no compiler or optimisation flags, so it falls short of A; first-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are from Google's July 2011 page (LevelDB revision 39 vs SQLite 3.7.6.3 and Kyoto Cabinet 1.2.67 TreeDB), first-party, with the benchmark code in the repo; compiler and optimisation flags are not stated, so the tier is C. The SQLite side was reasonably tuned (WAL, exclusive locking mode, reused prepared statements, a 4 MB cache of 1024-byte pages) but is a 2011 release, and the baseline runs have synchronous writes off for every engine. LevelDB loses on random reads (129,000 ops/s vs 134,000 for SQLite3 and 151,000 for Kyoto TreeDB) and with 100,000-byte values (1,100 vs 1,600 ops/s sequential and 480 vs 1,600 random writes). Synchronous writes are near parity on ext3 (100 vs 88 ops/s), and the page says ext4 drops LevelDB to about 31 sync writes per second while SQLite3 does not noticeably drop, so on ext4 SQLite3 wins synchronous writes. RocksDB and LMDB, the other category baselines, are not in this benchmark. The README says the repository receives very limited maintenance (only critical fixes and changes needed by internal clients are reviewed). Mozilla's kvbench (mykmelez/kvbench, Rust bindings) measured LMDB opening a database about 8x faster than LevelDB, while LevelDB was faster on a single synchronous 1-byte put (58.691 us vs 114.74 us).

notes: All claimed numbers and derived ratios match doc/benchmark.html (seq reads 10.5x, seq writes 16.0x, random writes 16.6x, batch random writes 10x vs SQLite3), and the losses (random reads, large values) are recorded. Fixed baseline_in_list to true (SQLite is in the embedded-kv baseline list) and replaced a caveat sentence that named std::map as a suggested baseline. Metadata checks out: BSD-3-Clause, about 39.5k stars, last commit 2026-03-11, active but README declares very limited maintenance; record shortcomings: 2011 numbers, compiler and flags unstated, loses random reads and large values, ext4 sync writes slower than SQLite.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark by the Infinity authors with a public driver (python/benchmark/run.py plus clients/ and configs/) and a stated CPU (Intel Core i5-13500H), but no compiler or flags: every engine runs from a Docker image, Infinity from the floating infiniflow/infinity:nightly tag while the table says v0.2.0. Missing compiler and flags fails A, and first-party numbers with partial methodology are C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Enwiki full-text (33M documents, 16 Python clients): 13731 QPS vs 1340 for Elasticsearch (10.2x, derived from page data) and 179 for Quickwit; P95 latency 1.37 ms vs 14.75 ms (10.8x, derived); insert and build index 1562 s vs 2289 s (1.5x, derived); memory 10.0 GB vs 21.0 GB. SIFT1M (top 100): 16320 QPS vs 934 for Elasticsearch (17.5x, derived) and 1303 for Qdrant (12.5x, derived) at recall 0.973 vs 0.992 and 0.979. GIST1M: 2200 QPS vs 305 and 339 (7.2x and 6.5x, derived) at recall 0.946 vs 0.885 and 0.947. Infinity is slower than Qdrant at insert and index build (74 s vs 46 s on SIFT1M, 463 s vs 366 s on GIST1M) and uses more disk on SIFT1M (792 MB vs 418 MB).
corrections.workload: Repo benchmark doc (docs/references/benchmark.md): 100,000 generated full-text OR queries (top 10) on 33M English Wikipedia documents with 16 Python clients, and L2 top-100 vector search on SIFT1M (10,000 queries) and GIST1M (1,000 queries), reporting QPS, recall, P95 latency, index build time, memory and disk; the vector tables do not state the client count (the doc's commands use 16).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated: all engines run from Docker images (elasticsearch:8.13.4 with ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xms16384m -Xmx32000m, qdrant/qdrant:v1.9.2, quickwit/quickwit:0.8.1, infiniflow/infinity:nightly); no build flags for Infinity.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark by the Infinity authors on one laptop-class CPU (i5-13500H, 32 GB). The table names Infinity v0.2.0 (about 2024) but the run command uses the floating infiniflow/infinity:nightly image and the current release is 0.7.x, so the measured build is not pinned. The vector comparison is not like for like: Infinity's SIFT config builds HNSW (M 16, ef_construction 200, ef 200) with LVQ 8-bit encoding, while Elasticsearch and Qdrant index float32 vectors with default search settings (Elasticsearch num_candidates 200), and Infinity's SIFT1M recall (0.973) is below both. Queries come from Python clients that talk HTTP/JSON to Elasticsearch and Qdrant (the Qdrant client does not enable gRPC) but Thrift to Infinity, so client-side serialisation may account for part of the QPS gap. Elasticsearch gets -Xmx32000m on a 32 GB machine, leaving little memory for the OS page cache Lucene relies on; Lucene itself is not measured separately. Infinity loses to Qdrant on vector index build time and SIFT1M disk use. None of the category's listed baselines (B-tree/LSM in RocksDB, LevelDB, LMDB, SQLite; learned indexes) is measured. The README headline claims (0.1 ms vector latency and 15K+ QPS; 1 ms and 12K+ QPS full-text on 33M documents) are in the same range as the doc table.

notes: Numbers match the doc table, but tier A was not justified: no compiler or flags, Docker nightly image, first-party, so C. Shortcomings to record: first-party, unpinned nightly build, LVQ-quantised index vs float32 competitors at lower recall, HTTP/JSON vs Thrift client protocols, Elasticsearch heap set to machine RAM, slower than Qdrant at index build; baseline_in_list set to false because Elasticsearch is not an indexes-category baseline, and the full-text comparison against Elasticsearch (Lucene) fits text-search-and-indexing better than indexes, so consider a category override. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, about 4.7k stars, last commit 2026-09-23, active.
